paragraphs: Hello. I am 薫瑞生, and from February this year I studied for ten weeks at the Medical University of Vienna. Without further ado, I would like to write about my life abroad.

My clerkship started in anesthesiology. In the first week I belonged to Group 4, one of the four OP groups, which handles ophthalmology, orthopedics and trauma, and I mainly accompanied anesthesia for orthopedics and trauma. Mornings in Vienna are very early, and the anesthesiology conference starts at 7:30, after which I would start the day's clerkship by asking the doctor in charge of whichever of the eight operating rooms interested me. Before going to Vienna I had been rather complacent, thinking that I could manage in English, but when I got there the surgical schedule, the locations of the operating rooms and the doctors' names were all in German, and since I was also the only student, I had a very hard time getting the hang of things. Fortunately, on the third day I met a good anesthesiologist who had come from the neurosurgery operating room, and by sticking to the operations he was in charge of I was able to place IV lines and arterial lines in quite a few cases, and I also performed tracheal intubation without a video laryngoscope in several cases, which I had heard even the students here were not easily allowed to do, and I was allowed to practise epidural anesthesia, so I could learn many things. In the second week, through this doctor's arrangement, I did my clerkship in the neurosurgery operating room, and it was also good to learn anesthesia in which, unlike in orthopedics, more delicate attention must be paid to position changes, drug doses and vital signs. In my last assigned operation in particular, in addition to peripheral lines and intubation, I was also entrusted with managing the vital signs, and being able to give anesthesia while thinking about the monitor values and the progress of the operation and checking with the doctor gave me the greatest confidence and experience.

When anesthesiology ended, my clerkship in obstetrics within obstetrics and gynecology began. Of ten days, four days were in the cesarean section and natural delivery rooms, and the rest I observed outpatient clinics and the ward. The first cesarean started at 8:00 and there were about five or six a day. I was surprised that each cesarean took a very short time, because the suturing method differed from Japan and the time to administer anesthesia was short. Between operations I attended natural deliveries, so it was a dizzying clerkship, but the sight of the baby I had been holding while the mother was being treated opening its gray eyes for the first time truly healed everything. I was also able to observe the treatment of two emergency patients with massive postpartum genital bleeding. In the outpatient clinic, since obstetrics at the Medical University of Vienna is among the largest in Europe and patients gather from all over the world, there were subdivided examination rooms such as for patients with maternal risk (DM, advanced maternal age and so on), patients at risk of chromosomal abnormality, and patients with fetal risk (suspected Down syndrome and so on), and I went through all of them for a day or two each. What left the strongest impression on me among them was induced abortion. In Japan, 22 weeks is regarded as the limit for being able to receive an induced abortion, but in Austria, when the mother and fetus are healthy, abortion is only available up to 12 weeks, while if a problem is found in either, abortion can be done at any time. I was allowed to witness the pretreatment to cause the death of a 25-week fetus in the womb. The doctor confirmed several times whether I really wanted to see it, and I too approached it with a certain resolve, but I immediately realised that my resolve had been naive. I cannot write the details, but it became an opportunity to think again about pro-life and pro-choice, which are said to be the ethical problems associated with abortion.

For the next two weeks I went to radiology. Because this hospital has so many wards and operations, there are CT, MRI and X-ray rooms divided over three floors, and I observed these rooms, esophageal contrast studies and the ICU after transplantation. This was the only part of this clerkship in which a supervising doctor was assigned, and that doctor looked after me very well, teaching me and having me practise image reading with real cases. This university is famous for transplantation, and a great many patients receive lung, liver, kidney and heart transplants, so it was fresh to learn radiological images that differ from normal anatomy and to see the postoperative course of transplants. Also, because the reading room is next to the imaging room, I found it interesting that the radiologist checks the captured images each time if necessary and takes images while instructing the technician on positioning and imaging method, and that sometimes, even in the middle of imaging, for a patient judged to have a poor life prognosis even with treatment, the radiologist can make the decision to stop imaging and send the patient home.

Next I returned to obstetrics and gynecology, this time in gynecology. It was during Easter holidays, so only about half the usual number of doctors were there and hands were short, so there were days when I kept drawing blood from the patients who came, using my halting German and English, and I felt it was rewarding. In this gynecology department breast cancer occupied a large portion, and I was also able to examine several patients. My knowledge of the breast was only what is written in books, and when asked "How was the palpation?" I could not at first answer with confidence, but the doctor in charge explained very carefully with images, and I learned a great deal. In gynecology in particular I could catch a glimpse of the immigration problem that Austria faces. Sometimes people from small ethnic groups who could speak neither English nor German and could not even use Google Translate came to the hospital, and there were also people who, although they had lived in Austria for decades, could not speak German and were examined through acquaintances or their children. I felt that it is a big problem that as immigrants increase and communities of each country form, people have become able to live without blending into Austria, and since immigrants are also increasing in Japan now, I felt the need to prepare medical care for such people.

I spent the last two weeks in plastic surgery. I had chosen this department because I had wanted to try a clerkship in a department that is called the star and is popular abroad, and because reconstructive surgery is thriving in Germany, I thought I might see something similar and be able to practise suturing, but when I got there, much of the surgery was what would be classified as cosmetic surgery in Japan, such as body lifts to remove the excess skin after people with severe obesity lose weight, and reduction of gynecomastia caused by thyroid disease, and I was surprised that it was done with insurance coverage. It was different from the surgery I had imagined, but even so it was good that I could observe the management and skin grafting of several people with severe burns over their whole bodies, such as I had never seen. As one would expect of the department said to be the most competitive, these last two weeks let me infer various things, such as that the doctors' job hunting seemed quite hard, that there was a somewhat severe atmosphere, and that, unlike other departments, there were only doctors from German-speaking countries.

Looking back, I think my exchange study abroad started with great bewilderment and a sense of mismatch. Studying abroad was a dream I had long pictured, and having prepared to a reasonable extent by studying medical English and acquiring in advance the procedures that I thought would be necessary, I came with quite a lot of tension, hoping to learn much and make friends abroad. But when I actually went, partly because the holidays overlapped, I hardly got to know any local students, and because I did not understand German, I could not judge from the conversation around me what was happening, I was refused entry into surgery, and I went to a place I had been told about and no one was there, and I was at a loss before walls that I would never run into in clerkships in Japan, and sometimes I lost confidence about whether I was really growing by coming all this way and whether I was gaining something that would lead to my future. But what I think now that I am back here is that it was truly a good experience. Because it was not an environment where I was allowed to do anything, I learned not only to ask actively but also to keep asking again and again without being discouraged even when told no, and, because the chances given are few, the importance of succeeding in that one chance and showing that I can do it. I myself had practised knot tying, suturing, IV access and tracheal intubation in Japan and gradually became able to do them to a certain extent, and I think I was fortunate to be given relatively many opportunities to be entrusted with procedures. Also, the cafes I went to after the clerkships, the opera house and theaters I went to after getting cheap tickets by using my student status, the short trips on weekends and holidays, and the "amusing" drug addicts who hung around the station nearest my apartment surely colored these short 3 months to make them last a lifetime.

Finally, I would like to lay down my pen by expressing my gratitude to Dr. 長谷川, Dr. Itzel, the professors who taught in the pre-departure training, and, above all, my family, who were my emotional support during the many days when things did not go well and who gave me unstinting support despite the yen's continuing sharp depreciation (it rose by nearly 20 yen during my time abroad...). Thank you.
